description: We are a passionate group of space enthusiasts, storytellers, and tech builders working on "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars." Our mission is to turn real aerospace data, historic mission logs, and forgotten off-world hardware into an interactive, unforgettable digital experience.
summary:
Abandoned, but not forgotten” is a one-page interactive story site that introduces school-age space fans, about ages 10 to 14, to hardware NASA has left on the Moon and Mars. Students start with a trade-off game: an Apollo astronaut can bring only three of five items home, so they see why equipment gets left behind. They then meet three machines, Surveyor 3, Opportunity and Ingenuity, through short stories, three mini-labs on time, dust and flight, and a tech lab where they tap each machine’s parts to learn what they did. Each story compares what engineers planned with what actually happened, such as Opportunity’s 90 planned Martian days against about 5,111 worked.

The project answers the challenge by turning real NASA mission records into hands-on learning about engineering trade-offs, rather than a simple list of objects. It matters because it shows young learners that a machine left behind is still a source of science, history and inspiration for future missions.
details:
What it does and how it works. “Abandoned, but not forgotten” is a one-page interactive web story for school-age space fans, about ages 10 to 14. It opens with a short game: an Apollo astronaut can carry only three of five items home from the Moon, so students feel why equipment gets left behind. They then meet three machines, Surveyor 3 on the Moon and Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars. Each story compares what engineers planned with what happened (for example, 90 planned Martian days against about 5,111 worked for Opportunity, and 5 planned flights against 72 for Ingenuity). Three mini-labs let students try time, dust and flight, and a tech lab lets them pick a machine and tap its parts to see what each one did.

Benefits and intended impact. The project turns mission records into hands-on learning about engineering trade-offs, which the challenge asks for, rather than a list of objects. We want students to see that a machine left behind is still a source of science, history and inspiration for future missions.

Tools. The page is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no outside libraries, and it works without sign-up. The fonts are Bricolage Grotesque and Atkinson Hyperlegible, loaded from Google Fonts. The demo is a 7-slide deck.

Creativity. The trade-off game comes first, so students start by making the choices engineers faced. Each story then shows planned versus actual results, so the surprise is visible.

Factors we considered. Accuracy: facts come from NASA and JPL pages, and we left out disputed claims. Accessibility: a readable typeface, large buttons that work with a keyboard, light and dark themes, and reduced motion for people who prefer it. Age: plain language, short pieces, and no images of people.
